questions.question_text: Which description defines a cubic metre?

options.text: the volume of a cube with metre-long edges
the area of a square with metre-long sides
options.why: Describes one square metre of area, not a three-dimensional volume.

options.text: the volume of a cube with three-metre edges
options.why: Uses the exponent as an edge length instead of a unit dimension.

options.text: the length of a one-metre line
options.why: Describes length in one dimension only.

questions.solution_text:
**Identify the space or unit being described.**
Define a cubic metre.

**Use the cubic-metre unit or compare the sizes.**
Use a cube with every edge one metre long.

**Record the answer and explain.**
Choose the volume of a cube with metre-long edges.

questions.question_text: Which object is best measured in m$^3$?

options.why: Uses a large-volume unit for a small object.
Uses a large-volume unit for a desk-sized object.
Uses a large-volume unit for a centimetre-sized object.

questions.solution_text:
**Identify the space or unit being described.**
Compare the sizes of the objects.

**Use the cubic-metre unit or compare the sizes.**
The moving van has a large interior space.

**Record the answer and explain.**
Choose the moving van; the other objects are small.

questions.question_text:
A space is filled by $42$ cubic-metre units.
How should its volume be recorded?

options.why: Uses square metres, which record area rather than a count of cubic units.
Uses metres, which record one-dimensional length rather than volume.
Changes the metre-sized units into centimetre-sized units without conversion.

questions.solution_text:
**Identify the space or unit being described.**
There are $42$ cubic-metre units.

**Use the cubic-metre unit or compare the sizes.**
Each contributes $1\text{ m}^3$.

**Record the answer and explain.**
Record $42\text{ m}^3$.

questions.question_text: Which is the more sensible estimate for a classroom?

options.why: Kept the cubic unit but chose centimetres; $150\text{ cm}^3$ is about the size of a small drink bottle, far too small for a room.
Used the squared unit for area instead of the cubed unit, so this measures floor space rather than the space inside the room.
Made both slips at once: chose the squared unit for area and the centimetre instead of the metre, giving a patch smaller than a page.

questions.solution_text:
**Identify the space or unit being described.**
Choose a plausible classroom volume.

**Use the cubic-metre unit or compare the sizes.**
A classroom contains many metre-sized cubes.

**Record the answer and explain.**
$150\text{ m}^3$ is sensible; $150\text{ cm}^3$ is tiny and square units measure area.

questions.question_text: Which method is suitable for estimating a classroom’s volume in cubic metres?

options.text: Estimate length, width and height in metres and combine the three dimensions.
Measure only the floor length and width in metres.
options.why: Measures the floor area but omits the classroom’s height.

options.text: Add the room’s length, width and height and write m$^3$.
options.why: Adds the dimensions instead of using them to count three-dimensional cubic units.

options.text: Measure one wall in centimetres and write the result as m$^3$.
options.why: Uses one surface and inconsistent units rather than all three metre dimensions.

questions.solution_text:
**Identify the space or unit being described.**
Estimate the room’s three-dimensional space.

**Use the cubic-metre unit or compare the sizes.**
Estimate length, width and height in metres; use cubes per layer and layers for a rectangular space.

**Record the answer and explain.**
Choose the method including all three dimensions, not floor area, their sum or one wall.

questions.question_text: Why is m$^2$ unsuitable for the amount of space inside a room?

options.text: It measures area, not three-dimensional volume.
It is always larger than m$^3$.
options.why: Compares unlike measurement types as if one were always numerically larger.

options.text: It can measure only curved objects.
options.why: Invents a shape restriction that square metres do not have.
Confuses square metres with capacity units.

questions.solution_text:
**Identify the space or unit being described.**
The space has length, width and height.

**Use the cubic-metre unit or compare the sizes.**
Square metres measure area in two dimensions.

**Record the answer and explain.**
Choose: area is different from three-dimensional volume.
